turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through, Mrs Hale. Sorry about the wait, the clinic's running late.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh I didn't mind. I was watching a toddler try to eat a magazine in the waiting room. Reminded me of my grandson, except he's sixteen now and eats the fridge.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha. What can I do for you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Karen made me come. My daughter. She thinks I'm falling to bits.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): She rang this morning. The note says two falls.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't fall. I slid. Twice, all right, but it's not the same thing. My legs just sort of gave and I went down the wall onto the carpet.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): So twice you ended up on the floor, and you'd rather we call it sliding.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Once in the kitchen, reaching for the biscuit tin. Once by the telly, getting up for the remote. No ambulance, no fuss.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you black out at all, either time?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I was wide awake. Cross with myself, mostly.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you hit your head?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I didn't.

[SEG0013] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Excuse me, doctor. I took the call from the daughter. She says the first time Mrs Hale hit the back of her head on the cupboard door, and she felt a lump later that evening.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Karen wasn't in the house! She turned up after I'd had my tea. There was no lump. She's dreadful for exaggerating.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right, you and she disagree about the head, and I'll record both. Any headache afterwards?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No headache. I watched Countdown and had a digestive.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain when it happened?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heart racing, palpitations?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. My heart's fine. It's my knees that are antique.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): She also said you go dizzy when you stand up. Is that fair?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yes. Off the sofa, the room goes swimmy for a few seconds. If I grab the mantelpiece it passes.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's that been happening?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight, I'd say. Maybe. I don't keep a diary.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Daughter's version is longer. She told me it started at the beginning of the month, so about four weeks. She's got it in her phone.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That's her figure. I'm saying a couple of weeks. And the beginning of the month I was busy with the hydrangeas, not my blood pressure. They're a lovely blue this year.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave it as somewhere between a fortnight and four weeks, not pinned down. Can you date the first slide?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. I can't. It was a bin day, so a Tuesday, but I don't know which Tuesday. Last week, the week before, I honestly couldn't tell you.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fine, date unknown. Sick with the dizziness? Nausea?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Appetite's perfectly good. Too good. There was Victoria sponge at the church coffee morning and I didn't say no.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your tablets. Blood pressure ones first.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): The white one is amlodipine, five milligrams. Been on it for years. And there's the water tablet in the morning.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry, the repeat slip says amlodipine ten milligrams once daily. That's what's on the summary, ten, not five.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten? The young doctor told me five. I don't cut them in half or anything. I haven't brought the box, that's the trouble. I'm sure it's five.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then we don't have an agreed dose for the amlodipine. I'll leave it blank till I see the packet. The water tablet, do you know the name and the strength?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Two and a half milligrams, it's bendroflumethiazide, every morning with the tea. Except if I'm out in the garden early I sometimes forget it altogether, so not every day if I'm honest.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the bendroflumethiazide is prescribed every morning, but you're not sure you take it as regularly as that.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Most mornings. My sister's the one with the system, on metformin for her sugar, diabetes for years, never misses. She keeps pushing her biotin on me for my hair, and I haven't taken a single one.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Her metformin and her biotin stay hers. You've got high blood pressure yourself, though, ongoing?

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, years and years. At night I take the little oval sleeping tablet, zopiclone, I think seven point five milligrams, though it could be the smaller strength. I always get them muddled.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Zopiclone at night, strength maybe seven point five milligrams, not confirmed. Do you take it every night?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Every night, yes. Otherwise I'm awake at three worrying about the boiler, which is a whole other saga, don't get me started.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. Well, actually, my sister insists I had a rash with penicillin as a child. I don't remember it. It might just be one of her tales.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): So possibly penicillin, with a rash, but it's uncertain and we'll treat it as unconfirmed. Any operations?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): A hysterectomy, twenty-odd years ago. And the cataracts, both eyes, about five-ish years back. That's the lot.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoking? Alcohol?

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked, and a sherry at Christmas if someone's pouring. I live on my own since Derek went, though Karen looks in. I still walk to the little Tesco, unless it's raining sideways.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Blood pressures, when you want them. Lying, after five minutes, one hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-two, pulse seventy-six.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): That's not what the chemist got. Last Tuesday she told me one hundred and fifty-two over ninety. I wrote it on the calendar, in pencil.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): And standing, at one minute, one hundred and six over sixty-eight. Pulse ninety-four. She went a bit wobbly and held the couch.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks. That's a proper drop. Mrs Hale, your chemist reading and this lying reading don't agree, so I'm keeping both rather than averaging them into nonsense.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): The girl in the chemist was rushing. And Derek's old home cuff always read high, he was on goodness knows what for his heart.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look. Pulse in the chair is regular, about seventy-eight, no bruise on the scalp and none on the shins. Heart sounds are normal and the chest is clear. Your lips are quite dry.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): I told her there was no lump. I live on tea, doctor. Water's boring.

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tea doesn't quite do it. My working impression is postural dizziness from the blood pressure tablets. Provisional. The standing drop fits that, and I don't think this is a stroke.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh good. My mother had a stroke when she was eighty, and I've had that in the back of my mind all week.

[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll note your mother's stroke. What I'm changing is the water tablet: stop the bendroflumethiazide, two and a half milligrams, from today. Amlodipine stays as it is until we see the box, and the zopiclone stays but don't increase it.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop it altogether? Even on the days I remember?
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. If your ankles start to swell, phone us. I'd like kidney bloods and a sodium this week, and an ECG as well, just to be thorough.
[SEG0061] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can book the bloods for Thursday morning, and the ECG can be done in the same slot if the machine's free.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday's meant to be the hairdresser. Oh, all right, Thursday. Can it be early? I'm hopeless after lunch.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Early Thursday is fine. And I want to see you back here in a fortnight, results or no results.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. I'll bring the amlodipine box, shall I? And the sleeping tablets, so you can read the strength.

[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring every box. Stand up in stages, sit on the edge of the bed first, and if you feel a slide coming, sit on the floor on purpose. No driving while you're swimmy. More fluid than just tea.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop the water tablet, drink more water, don't drive, come back in a fortnight. I'll tell Karen to stand down. Thanks, love.

spec.situation: Older patient who fell twice 'but not really fell, slid down'; dizzy on standing; takes several BP and sleeping tablets; daughter reports what the patient minimises; nurse reads lying and standing BP; doctor changes one tablet.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

omissions.text: The two slide/fall episodes occurred once in the kitchen while reaching for the biscuit tin and once by the television when getting up for the remote; she went down the wall onto the carpet.

Amlodipine on the repeat slip was specifically recorded as 10 mg once daily; the recorded medication entry for amlodipine is missing the once-daily frequency and the documented 10 mg from the summary as part of the discrepancy.
Zopiclone dose is uncertain and may be the smaller strength; recording it simply as 7.5 mg is overstated because the patient was unsure.
No known drug allergies was stated before the uncertain childhood penicillin rash history; this broader NKDA statement is not recorded.

Standing blood pressure was taken at one minute and she became symptomatic on standing, but there is no record that the lying blood pressure was after five minutes in the procedures/actions context beyond the vital sign entry.

The doctor documented uncertainty about the head injury by saying he would record both versions because the patient and daughter disagreed; this explicit disagreement/plan to record both is not captured as such.
The doctor advised amlodipine should stay unchanged until the medication box is checked; that explicit plan for amlodipine is not recorded as a clinical action.
